target: AG1's claim that alternative energies can effectively replace fossil fuels, especially in large-country systems
objection: In the U.S., alternative energy use has never exceeded 20% historically, so AG1's replacement claim is not supported by large-country real-world performance. AG2 argues that this shows alternatives have not effectively displaced fossil fuels at the scale needed in practice.

target: AG1's assumption that nuclear can help replace fossil fuels
objection: Nuclear energy is too dangerous and ineffective to be a serious solution to global warming. AG2 says accidents like Fukushima wipe out the carbon-free electricity gains, so nuclear cannot be relied on as a quick firm low-carbon substitute.

target: AG1's implication that natural gas is unnecessary for transition
objection: Natural gas is a fossil fuel that AG2 says is an appropriate and necessary bridge fuel to meet net-zero goals, because existing gas infrastructure enables faster emissions reductions than waiting for a full alternative buildout.

target: AG1's claim that historical low renewable/nuclear shares do not show impossibility
objection: AG2 argues that because U.S. alternative energy use has historically stayed below 20%, alternatives have not scaled enough in large-country practice to count as an effective replacement, so historical experience supports skepticism about near-term replacement.

target: AG1's claim that fossil bridge use is compatible with effective replacement
objection: AG2 rejects the idea that keeping natural gas as a bridge still counts as effective replacement, arguing that a realistic net-zero pathway requires fossil fuels to remain in the system during transition, so alternatives are not an all-at-once replacement.

target: AG1's claim that nuclear can reliably support the transition
objection: AG2 repeats that nuclear is too dangerous and ineffective, so it cannot be counted on as a dependable firm complement that would enable alternatives to replace fossil fuels effectively.

target: AG1's claim that accelerated low-carbon buildout can displace fossil capacity in large countries
objection: AG2 argues that U.S. historical experience shows alternatives have not scaled to a level that would materially displace fossil fuels in large-country practice, so the near-to-medium-term displacement claim is not credible.

target: AG1's argument that grid reliability can be maintained without fossil fuels using non-fossil flexibility and firm low-carbon resources
objection: AG2 contends that large systems require substantial firm/dispatchable capacity, and that there is evidence a large country cannot build enough non-fossil flexibility and firm low-carbon capacity fast enough for transition needs, so fossil generation remains necessary for reliability.

target: AG1's claim that nuclear can replace fossil gas in the near-to-medium term
objection: AG2 says nuclear is too dangerous and ineffective to serve as a fast, reliable firm low-carbon resource, so it cannot displace the fossil-gas role that AG1 says it can.

target: AG1's claim that renewables plus nuclear can make fossil-gas bridging unnecessary for grid reliability
objection: AG2 maintains that variable renewables need substantial dispatchable backup and that natural gas is the practical bridge fuel when firm low-carbon capacity is insufficient, so fossil bridging is unavoidable in the near-to-medium term.

target: AG1's claim that alternatives can also replace fossil fuels outside electricity, including industrial heat and feedstocks
objection: AG2 argues that fossil fuels are used for industrial process heat and chemical feedstocks, and renewables do not directly provide those services at scale without major new technologies and infrastructure, so alternatives cannot yet effectively replace fossil fuels across all major uses.

target: AG1's claim that renewables and low-carbon electricity can power industrial heat and feedstock substitutes
objection: AG2 says renewable-derived hydrogen and e-fuels require much more electricity because of conversion losses, and U.S.-style historical alternative-energy shares show large countries cannot yet scale the extra electricity needed fast enough, so non-electric industrial fossil uses will not be fully replaced soon.

target: AG1's claim that large countries can scale the electricity needed for hydrogen and e-fuels fast enough
objection: AG2 says there is no evidence large countries can scale low-carbon electricity quickly enough to cover the expanded demand created by hydrogen/e-fuel conversion losses, so the assumption that such scaling is feasible is not warranted.

target: AG1's claim that high-renewable electricity grids show industrial fossil uses can be displaced
objection: AG2 replies that high renewable shares in countries like Iceland, Paraguay, Costa Rica, and Norway only show decarbonized electricity, not operationally scaled renewable hydrogen/e-fuels or heavy-industry replacement, so those examples do not prove fossil industrial services can be replaced at national scale.

target: AG1's claim that renewable energy already displaces fossil industrial services in practice
objection: AG2 argues that the target has no evidence that renewable substitution already displaces fossil industrial services at large-country scale, so the inference that alternatives can replace fossil fuels broadly in practice is unwarranted.

target: AG1's claim that renewable electricity and hydrogen can replace fossil chemical feedstocks
objection: AG2 says hydrogen does not supply the carbon atoms needed for most chemical feedstocks, so renewables plus hydrogen/e-fuels cannot fully replace fossil feedstocks without a large-scale non-fossil carbon supply that does not yet exist.

target: AG1's claim that captured-CO2 plus green-hydrogen synthesis can displace fossil feedstocks soon
objection: AG2 argues that building the full chain—hydrogen production, CO2 capture/conditioning/delivery, and synthesis plants—has long lead times and bottlenecks, so the proposed pathway cannot be assumed to scale fast enough for near-to-medium-term replacement.

target: AG1's claim that the feedstock-substitution chain can be scaled incrementally without needing full buildout first
objection: AG2 says the interdependent components of the captured-CO2/green-H2 chain are bottlenecked by the slowest component, so the overall transition cannot be assumed to proceed quickly enough to avoid fossil feedstock use during the near-to-medium term.

target: AG1's claim that captured-CO2 substitution can be powered without fossil bridging
objection: AG2 argues that capture, conditioning, compression, electrolysis, and synthesis are energy-intensive and that low-carbon electricity is still too limited in large countries, so fossil energy—especially natural gas—will still be needed to run the substitution chain during transition.
